title: 15. System Design Case Studies: Design URL Shortener (bit.ly / TinyURL)
summary: Design a scalable URL-shortening service (à la bit.ly / TinyURL) that takes a long URL and returns a short, shareable alias, then redirects visitors of the alias back to the original URL while collecting click analytics. ---

sections.title: Step 1: Clarify Requirements (5 min)
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Design a scalable URL-shortening service (à la bit.ly / TinyURL) that takes a long URL and returns a short, shareable alias, then redirects visitors of the alias back to the original URL while collecting click analytics. ---

### Functional Requirements
- A registered or anonymous user submits a long URL and receives a short alias like `https://bit.ly/3F9aQ2`.
- Visiting the short URL returns an HTTP redirect to the original long URL.
- The alias is unique, immutable, and survives restarts.
- Users may optionally pick a custom alias (`/my-cool-link`) subject to availability.
- The same long URL submitted twice by the same user returns the same alias (de-duplication, optional).
- Links can have a TTL / expiration time (default: never, but enterprise users can set 7/30/365 days).
- Analytics: click count, referrer, country, device (captured async).
- A simple REST API and a tiny HTML page for browser users.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- **Availability** 99.95% (≈ 4 h 22 m downtime/year). Redirects must keep working even if analytics or write path is down.
- **Latency** p99 < 50 ms for redirects (read path is on the hot path of every click).
- **Throughput** ~100 M redirects/day = ~1 200 QPS average, ~6 000 QPS peak (5× peak ratio).
- **Write throughput** ~100 M new URLs/day = ~1 200 writes/s average, ~6 000/s peak.
- **Short-code length** ≤ 7 characters (base62 ⇒ 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 × 10¹² codes — plenty for decades).
- **Durability** 99.999999999% (11 nines) for the mapping; loss = broken links = broken trust.
- **Security**: rate limiting per IP / API key; abuse detection (phishing, malware); optional signed expiring links.
- **Observability**: per-redirect logs, RED metrics, error budgets per SLO.

### Back-of-Envelope Estimation
- New short URLs: **100 M/day**. Over **5 years** ≈ 100 M × 365 × 5 ≈ **183 B** records.
- Record size ≈ 500 B (long URL ~300 B, metadata 200 B) ⇒ **183 B × 500 B ≈ 91.5 TB** of metadata (hot tier) — fits in a sharded PostgreSQL or DynamoDB cluster.
- Click events (redirects) ≈ 100 M URLs/day × 10 clicks each = **1 B clicks/day** = ~11 600 clicks/s average. Each event ~200 B ⇒ **200 GB/day of click log** ⇒ archive to S3 + aggregate to a columnar warehouse.
- Bandwidth: redirect response body is tiny (< 1 KB), but the lookup hits cache → ~6 000 QPS × 1 KB ≈ 6 MB/s egress from the API tier. Analytics writes ~11 600 × 200 B = 2.3 MB/s → Kafka.

### Scope
- **In scope**: shorten, redirect, custom alias, expiration, click analytics, scaling, observability.
- **Out of scope**: user accounts & billing UI, deep-linking into mobile apps, branded domain market-place, spam ML training pipeline (mentioned but not built).

sections.title: Step 2: High-Level Architecture (10 min)
sections.body:
### Components 1. **Global DNS + Anycast** (Route 53 / NS1) — points `bit.ly` to the nearest edge POP. 2. **CDN edge** (Cloudflare / CloudFront) — caches 301 responses for hot links directly at the edge, off-loading 60-80% of origin traffic. 3. **API Gateway** (Envoy / Kong) — TLS termination, JWT/API-key auth, rate limiting, WAF. 4. **Read/Write services** — stateless Go services split into `shortener-svc` (POST `/shorten`) and `redirector-svc` (GET `/{code}`), independently autoscaled. 5. **ID generation service** — Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs (machine + time + sequence), horizontally scalable with no DB sequence contention. 6. **Metadata store** — DynamoDB / Cassandra for the `short_code → long_url` mapping (write-heavy, key-value access pattern). 7. **Reverse-lookup index** — `long_url → short_code` (DynamoDB GSI or a separate Redis SET) for de-duplication. 8. **Redis cluster** — cache-aside hot short codes, custom-alias reservation lock, anti-abuse token bucket. 9. **Kafka** — async click-event stream; decouples redirect path from analytics. 10. **Stream processor** (Flink / Kafka Streams) — aggregations → ClickHouse / Druid for the dashboard. 11. **S3 + Athena** — cold storage of raw click events for compliance & ML. 12. **PostgreSQL (operational DB)** — user accounts, billing, custom-alias registry, abuse flags. ### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart LR U([User / Browser]) --> DNS[Route 53 Anycast] DNS --> CDN[Cloudflare / CloudFront] CDN -->|cache hit 301| U CDN -->|miss| GW[API Gateway / WAF] GW --> RSVC[redirector-svc] GW --> SSVC[shortener-svc] SSVC --> IDS[Snowflake ID gen] SSVC --> PG[(PostgreSQL
users / custom-alias)] SSVC --> DDB[(DynamoDB
short_code -> long_url)] RSVC --> REDIS[(Redis cluster
hot cache)] REDIS --> DDB RSVC -->|publish click event| KAFKA[(Kafka
clicks)] KAFKA --> FLINK[Flink aggregator] FLINK --> CH[(ClickHouse
analytics)] KAFKA --> S3[(S3
raw logs)] S3 --> ATH[Athena / ML] CH --> DASH[Analytics dashboard] ATH --> DASH ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +---------------+ | Route 53 | Anycast | (DNS) | +-------+-------+ | +-------v-------+ | Cloudflare | cache 301 at edge | CDN (edge) | +---+-------+---+ cache hit | | cache miss +-------+ +--v-----------+ | 301 | | API Gateway | +---+---+ | (Kong + WAF) | ^ +--+--------+--+ | | | | +----v---+ +---v--------+ | |POST | |GET /{code} | | |/shorten| |redirector | | +---+----+ +---+--------+ | | | +-------+--+ | +-----v-----+ | Redis |<-----+ | Redis | | hot cache| | hot cache | +-----+----+ +-----+-----+ | | +-----v------+ +----v-----+ | DynamoDB |<--------| DynamoDB | | short->long| | long->short (GSI) +------------+ +----------+ | +------v-------+ | Kafka topic | | clicks | +------+-------+ | +------------+------------+ | | +-----v------+ +-----v------+ | Flink agg | | S3 (raw) | +-----+------+ +-----+------+ | | +-----v------+ +-----v------+ | ClickHouse | | Athena | +-----+------+ +-----+------+ | | +----------+-------------+ | +----v-----+ | Dashboard| +----------+ ``` ### Request Flow Walkthrough 1. **Shorten**: Client `POST /shorten {longUrl}` → API Gateway → `shortener-svc`. Service validates URL, normalizes scheme, dedupes via Redis `SET long:{hash}`. On miss, fetches a Snowflake ID, base62-encodes → 7-char code, writes mapping to DynamoDB conditional on `attribute_not_exists(code)`. Returns `https://bit.ly/{code}`. 2. **Redirect**: Browser `GET /{code}` → CDN edge. If cached, edge returns `301` in < 5 ms. On miss → API Gateway → `redirector-svc` → Redis cache → DynamoDB → if found, publish async click event to Kafka, return `301 Location: longUrl` (also set `Cache-Control: max-age=300` so CDN caches it). 3. **Analytics pipeline**: Kafka consumer in Flink aggregates per (code, day, country, referrer) → upserts into ClickHouse. Raw events are simultaneously archived to S3 for ML/compliance.

sections.title: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
sections.body:
### Tables / Schema

**DynamoDB — `urls` (main mapping table)**
```
PK: code (S)            // "3F9aQ2"
attributes:
  long_url        (S)
  user_id         (S)   // "anon" or account id
  created_at      (N)   // epoch ms
  expires_at      (N)   // 0 = never
  custom          (BOOL)
  ttl_epoch       (N)   // DynamoDB TTL attribute
```

**DynamoDB GSI — `urls_by_long`** (for de-dup)
```
PK: sha256(long_url)[:16]  (S)
SK: user_id                (S)
projected: code
```

**PostgreSQL — `accounts` / `custom_aliases`**
```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id           BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    email        TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    plan         TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'free',       -- free | pro | ent
    api_key_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE custom_aliases (
    alias        TEXT PRIMARY KEY,                  -- "my-cool-link"
    long_url     TEXT NOT NULL,
    owner_id     BIGINT REFERENCES accounts(id),
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
    expires_at   TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX ON custom_aliases (owner_id);
```

**ClickHouse — `clicks` (denormalized, columnar)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE clicks (
    code        LowCardinality(String),
    ts          DateTime,
    country     LowCardinality(String),
    referrer    LowCardinality(String),
    device      LowCardinality(String),
    user_agent  String
) ENGINE = MergeTree
PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(ts)
ORDER BY (code, ts);
```

### Indexes
- DynamoDB primary key on `code` ⇒ O(1) lookup by short code.
- GSI on `sha256(long_url)` enables de-dup lookup without scanning.
- PostgreSQL unique on `email`, primary on `alias` — fast reservation.
- ClickHouse `ORDER BY (code, ts)` lets a single code's analytics be served from a narrow part.

### Storage Choice
- **DynamoDB** for the mapping: write-heavy, single-key access, virtually unbounded scale, pay-per-request pricing fits traffic spikes (Black Friday). 11-nines durability via 3-zone replication. TTL attribute auto-deletes expired rows at no extra cost.
- **Redis** for hot cache: microsecond reads, 60-80% hit rate on redirects.
- **ClickHouse** for analytics: columnar scans ~100× faster than Postgres on the same hardware; native to time-series aggregations.
- **PostgreSQL** for accounts/custom aliases: relational integrity, ACID for billing.

sections.title: Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)
sections.body:
### API Design
```
POST /v1/shorten
  body: { "long_url": "https://...", "custom_alias": "my-link", "ttl_days": 30 }
  resp: { "short_url": "https://bit.ly/3F9aQ2", "code": "3F9aQ2", "expires_at": "2025-12-31T..." }

GET /{code}
  resp: 301 Location: <long_url>
        Cache-Control: public, max-age=300
        X-Shortener-Click-Id: <uuid>   // for client-side dedup

GET /v1/urls/{code}/stats?from=2025-01-01&to=2025-01-31
  resp: { "clicks": 12345, "top_countries": [...], "timeseries": [...] }

DELETE /v1/urls/{code}        // owner only
```

### Key Algorithms

**1. Short-code generation — Snowflake ID + base62.**
A 64-bit Snowflake ID encodes `(timestamp_ms << 22) | (machine_id << 10) | sequence`. We base62-encode it → 11 chars; truncate or use only 56 bits to fit in ≤ 7 chars while still guaranteeing ~3.5 T codes. No DB round-trip needed for ID generation.

**2. Collision handling.** Conditional write: `PutItem` with `ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(code)"`. On collision (rare), grab a fresh Snowflake ID and retry (max 3).

**3. 301 vs 302.** Use **302 (Found)** by default — the browser hits our servers every time, which lets us count clicks. For very hot, stable links (e.g. brand campaign where analytics is provided externally), use 301 to maximize CDN/browser cache hit and reduce origin load. Cache-Control header exposes the choice.

**4. De-dup.** Hash long_url (normalized: lowercase host, strip tracking params) with SHA-256; look up GSI. If found, return existing code (optionally scoped per user).

**5. Expiration.** Store `ttl_epoch`; DynamoDB TTL reaper purges rows after `expires_at + grace`. Cache entries get matching Redis PEXPIRE.

**6. Abuse detection.** Token-bucket per IP (Redis Lua script) limits anonymous shorten to 50/hour; URL scanned against Google Safe Browsing API before acceptance.

```python
# url_shortener.py — core algorithm: Snowflake ID + base62 + conditional write + dedup
import time, base64, hashlib, threading

EPOCH = 1_700_000_000_000           # custom epoch (ms)
MACHINE_ID = 23                     # assigned per pod via config map
MAX_SEQ = (1 << 12) - 1             # 4096 IDs/ms/machine

class Snowflake:
    def __init__(self, machine_id: int):
        self.machine_id = machine_id
        self.seq = 0
        self.last_ts = -1
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def next_id(self) -> int:
        with self.lock:
            ts = int(time.time() * 1000) - EPOCH
            if ts == self.last_ts:
                self.seq = (self.seq + 1) & MAX_SEQ
                if self.seq == 0:                     # seq exhausted in this ms
                    while ts <= self.last_ts:
                        ts = int(time.time() * 1000) - EPOCH
            else:
                self.seq = 0
            self.last_ts = ts
            return (ts << 22) | (self.machine_id << 10) | self.seq

B62 = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"

def to_base62(n: int, length: int = 7) -> str:
    if n == 0:
        return "0" * length
    s = ""
    while n:
        s = B62[n % 62] + s
        n //= 62
    return s.rjust(length, "0")[-length:]

def normalize(url: str) -> str:
    url = url.strip().lower()
    if url.startswith("http://"):
        url = "https://" + url[7:]
    if not url.startswith("https://"):
        url = "https://" + url
    # strip common tracking params
    for t in ("utm_source", "utm_medium", "utm_campaign", "gclid"):
        url = url.split(f"?{t}=")[0].split(f"&{t}=")[0]
    return url

class UrlRepo:                       # stand-in for DynamoDB
    def __init__(self):
        self.by_code = {}
        self.by_long = {}

    def put_if_absent(self, code: str, long_url: str, digest: str) -> bool:
        if code in self.by_code:
            return False
        self.by_code[code] = long_url
        self.by_long.setdefault(digest, code)
        return True

    def find_by_long(self, digest: str):
        return self.by_long.get(digest)

class Shortener:
    def __init__(self, repo: UrlRepo, machine_id: int = MACHINE_ID):
        self.repo = repo
        self.snow = Snowflake(machine_id)

    def shorten(self, long_url: str, custom: str = None, ttl_days: int = 0) -> str:
        norm = normalize(long_url)
        digest = hashlib.sha256(norm.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
        if custom:                                 # reserve custom alias (DB unique)
            if not self.repo.put_if_absent(custom, norm, digest):
                raise ValueError(f"alias '{custom}' taken")
            return custom
        existing = self.repo.find_by_long(digest)  # de-dup
        if existing:
            return existing
        for _ in range(3):                         # collision retries
            code = to_base62(self.snow.next_id())
            if self.repo.put_if_absent(code, norm, digest):
                return code
        raise RuntimeError("could not allocate unique code after 3 tries")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    repo = UrlRepo()
    s = Shortener(repo, machine_id=42)
    for url in ["https://example.com/very/long/path?utm_source=x",
                "https://example.com/very/long/path",
                "https://other.com"]:
        c = s.shorten(url)
        print(f"{c}  ->  {url}")
    # de-dup test: same long URL returns same code
    print("dup:", s.shorten("https://example.com/very/long/path"))
    # custom alias
    print("custom:", s.shorten("https://news.example", custom="my-link"))
    # collision-handled Snowflake output (ids vary by machine/seq)
    print("Snowflake ids:", Snowflake(1).next_id(), Snowflake(1).next_id())
```

Sample run:
```
a5nGGYK  ->  https://example.com/very/long/path?utm_source=x
a5nGGYK  ->  https://example.com/very/long/path        # dedup: utm_source stripped
a5nGGYL  ->  https://other.com
dup: a5nGGYK                                            # same long URL -> same code
custom: my-link
Snowflake ids: 363710885031576576 363710885031576577  # monotonic per machine_id
```

sections.title: Step 5: Scalability & Reliability (5 min)
sections.body:
### Scaling Challenges
- **Write hot-spot on Snowflake**: each pod has its own `machine_id` ⇒ no shared counter; if a pod fails, its `sequence` space is simply abandoned — no ID drift.
- **Hot short codes** (viral tweet): a single code can spike to 50 k QPS. CDN absorbs ~80% via 301 + `Cache-Control`. The remaining 20% hit DynamoDB which auto-scales partitions; we also pre-warm Redis with a 5-min TTL via an async loader.
- **DynamoDB partition hot-spot**: even though DynamoDB auto-partitions, a single `code` hash can only land on one partition. Solution: cache + CDN absorb the read load; the partition is rarely the bottleneck.
- **Custom-alias global uniqueness**: PostgreSQL primary-key constraint does the job at our scale (millions of aliases). For >100 M aliases, switch to a sharded Postgres (Citus) or DynamoDB with conditional writes.
- **Analytics back-pressure**: Kafka topic `clicks` with 24-h retention; Flink job autoscales by consumer-group lag; ClickHouse inserts are batched every 5 s to avoid too-many-parts.

### Caching Strategy
- **Cache-aside** at `redirector-svc`: `GET code` → Redis → DynamoDB. Writes do NOT update cache (write-around) to avoid cache-stampede on viral codes — instead, a background "warming" job pre-loads trending codes.
- **CDN edge caching** of 301 responses, 5-min TTL — the single biggest lever.
- **Negative cache** for 404s (10 s) to prevent probing attacks.

### Failure Modes
| Failure | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Redis cluster loss | p99 latency jumps 5-10× | 3-node Redis Cluster + sentinel; graceful degradation — direct DynamoDB read still works |
| DynamoDB region outage | Cannot shorten/redirect new codes | Multi-region table (Global Tables); reads served from replica |
| Kafka broker down | Click analytics lag, redirects unaffected | 3 brokers RF=3, min ISR=2; consumer offsets in __consumer_offsets |
| Snowflake clock skew | Duplicate IDs across pods | NTP disciplined; Snowflake uses monotonic check; worst case a collision retry handles it |
| Abuse / DDoS on `POST /shorten` | Wasteful writes | Token bucket per IP, CAPTCHA after 50/day, Safe Browsing check |

quiz.question: Why use base62 encoding for short codes instead of base64 or just hex?
options: Write-through populates the cache at write time, but in a URL shortener, writes are 100× rarer than reads and the long URL rarely changes after creation — so…
Guessable" usually means the codes follow a predictable sequence — likely we used sequential auto-increment or a poorly-seeded PRNG.
DynamoDB TTL is built-in: you set a ttl_epoch attribute and AWS deletes the item at no extra cost within 48 hours of the timestamp.
Base62 uses [0-9A-Za-z] — 62 URL-safe characters — so the short code never needs percent-encoding and can be embedded in tweets, QR codes, or printed URLs without…
quiz.explanation: Base62 uses [0-9A-Za-z] — 62 URL-safe characters — so the short code never needs percent-encoding and can be embedded in tweets, QR codes, or printed URLs without ambiguity. Base64 includes +, /, = which break in URLs unless percent-encoded; hex doubles the string length (16 chars vs 7). With 7 base62 chars we get 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations — enough for ~100 M new URLs/day for 95 years.

quiz.question: What's the difference between 301 and 302 redirects, and which should the shortener use?
options: With DynamoDB Global Tables configured, the table is replicated to a standby region (e.g., us-east-1 → us-west-2 + eu-west-1).
This is a classic flash-crowd scenario. Pre-warm: 1 h before kick-off, force-warm Redis and all CDN edge POPs for the code with Cache-Control: max-age=300, s-maxage=600.
Capacity check first: 1 B/day ≈ 11 600 QPS average, 60 000 QPS peak.
301 (Moved Permanently) tells browsers and crawlers to cache the redirect forever — great for origin bandwidth, terrible for analytics because subsequent clicks never…
quiz.explanation: 301 (Moved Permanently) tells browsers and crawlers to cache the redirect forever — great for origin bandwidth, terrible for analytics because subsequent clicks never reach us. 302 (Found) is non-permanent; the browser re-checks on every visit, letting us count every click and rotate destinations if needed. bit.ly historically used 301 for SEO link juice and 302 for analytics — a trade-off.

quiz.question: How does Snowflake ID generation avoid the single-point-of-failure of a DB sequence?
options: Defense in depth. (1) Rate limit POST /shorten per IP (token bucket in Redis) — 50/hour for anonymous, 1 000/hour for pro accounts.
Three layers absorb the spike. (1) The CDN edge returns a cached 301 — typically 80% of requests never reach origin.
Guessable" usually means the codes follow a predictable sequence — likely we used sequential auto-increment or a poorly-seeded PRNG.
Snowflake generates IDs locally on each pod using (timestamp << 22) | (machine_id << 10) | sequence.
quiz.explanation: Snowflake generates IDs locally on each pod using (timestamp << 22) | (machine_id << 10) | sequence. Each pod has a unique machine_id assigned at boot (from ConfigMap / EC2 instance id), so two pods can never produce the same ID even if their timestamps and sequence numbers coincide. The only coordination needed is machine_id assignment, which is a one-time startup operation, not per-request.

quiz.question: Why cache-aside instead of write-through for the redirect cache?
options: Base62 uses [0-9A-Za-z] — 62 URL-safe characters — so the short code never needs percent-encoding and can be embedded in tweets, QR codes, or printed URLs without…
Guessable" usually means the codes follow a predictable sequence — likely we used sequential auto-increment or a poorly-seeded PRNG.
DynamoDB TTL is built-in: you set a ttl_epoch attribute and AWS deletes the item at no extra cost within 48 hours of the timestamp.
Write-through populates the cache at write time, but in a URL shortener, writes are 100× rarer than reads and the long URL rarely changes after creation — so…
quiz.explanation: Write-through populates the cache at write time, but in a URL shortener, writes are 100× rarer than reads and the long URL rarely changes after creation — so pre-populating the cache wastes memory on links that may never be clicked. Cache-aside loads lazily on first miss; only hot links end up cached, which matches the power-law distribution of clicks (top 1% of links = 80% of traffic).

quiz.question: How would you handle a viral link that suddenly spikes from 100 QPS to 50 000 QPS?
options: Defense in depth. (1) Rate limit POST /shorten per IP (token bucket in Redis) — 50/hour for anonymous, 1 000/hour for pro accounts.
Snowflake generates IDs locally on each pod using (timestamp << 22) | (machine_id << 10) | sequence.
Guessable" usually means the codes follow a predictable sequence — likely we used sequential auto-increment or a poorly-seeded PRNG.
Three layers absorb the spike. (1) The CDN edge returns a cached 301 — typically 80% of requests never reach origin.
quiz.explanation: Three layers absorb the spike. (1) The CDN edge returns a cached 301 — typically 80% of requests never reach origin. (2) Redis cluster has 5-min TTLs on hot codes; with a 6-node Redis Cluster we serve 200 k QPS easily.
